summary: The tumour microenvironment (TME) is a multidimensional dynamic and complex system of cells and non-cellular components that not only drives tumour progression but also substantially influences response to therapy. Understanding TME biology for basic research and identifying biomarkers in the TME to stratify patients for therapy is crucial for optimizing therapeutic outcomes. Current standards for investigating TME dynamics, if even considered beyond preclinical work, rely predominantly on samples for tissue staining and sequencing and require invasive procedures to obtain tissue via surgery or biopsies. This leads to limited assessment of spatial heterogeneity and minimal temporal information as this depends on the timing of tissue sampling, which results in undefined clinical utility. Molecular imaging provides promising solutions by enabling non-invasive, real-time multidimensional spatiotemporal probing of the TME that can complement current ex vivo practices. This Review highlights the relevance of molecular imaging agents and methods that can effectively capture spatiotemporal TME characteristics in situ, offering critical insights into tumour behaviour and treatment response. We provide an overview of current preclinical imaging strategies and their applications in identifying cellular and non-cellular components of the TME, along with monitoring progression-associated processes and treatment response. We showcase new developments and avenues being explored in preclinical imaging, as well as offer perspectives into existing and emerging clinical imaging of the TME to enhance patient care and highlight opportunities for improvement. Overall, integrating TME imaging into clinical practice holds the potential to bridge critical gaps in spatiotemporal resolution, ultimately enabling more precise diagnosis, patient stratification and personalized therapeutic interventions. This Review discusses molecular imaging probes and modalities for studying the complexity and dynamics of the tumour microenvironment in preclinical research and further highlights emerging clinical applications in diagnostics and intervention.
